doc.title: Ken Peplowski interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997 [interview 1 of 2]

chapter: Dorsey band and moving to New York
title: Joining Buddy Morrow's Tommy Dorsey ghost band
summary: Invited to join at a Cleveland festival, two and a half years on the road, bus life, and the spotlight Morrow gave him.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: How did — your first big job, that you said man, I’ve been working towards this and this finally happened.

It’s kind of a two part thing. When I was living in Cleveland and I was playing of course in this polka band, and at the same time I started branching out and playing with jazz groups around town. Flash forward a few years, I’m in college. I get called to play at a jazz festival in Cleveland with my own group, and it’s me, the Teddy Wilson trio and the Tommy Dorsey band — a ghost band — but so anyway so I do this concert and it’s a big deal for me. And I got asked to join the Dorsey band that night by the leader, Buddy Morrow, who’s still on the band, over 20 years later now. He’s like an iron man. He’s this great trombone player who is eternally on the road and never practiced a day that I knew and picked up his horn cold and played the theme song, “I’m Getting Sentimental For You,” perfectly every night. And that was my big break. That got me out of Cleveland. I took a job on the road with that band. And even though it was a ghost band, at that time it was a really good band, and there were a lot of big bands still around. This was like the late 70s. All the bands were still around — Duke’s band and Basie and Buddy Rich, Woody Herman. And we were all in those circles. And that was a big deal for me because in fact my teacher in Cleveland, my clarinet teacher said to me when I was debating whether I should go on this job or not, he said, “look you can be a big fish in a small pond, or you can get out there and challenge yourself.” And that’s what I decided to do. And I was on that band for about two and a half years. A great time, a lot of hard work. We were traveling 48 weeks out of the year.

Mostly bus, oh, you know like we’d play the job, we’d do what we call “hit and runs.” We’d play the job, get on the bus twelve hours, next place. And then you get to the next town and we’re paying for our own rooms too.

Speaking of the glamorous life. So we’d do what we call “ghosting,” where you’d have one guy check in with a single, and then two others would sneak in the back way. You know and you’d make bets and whoever lost the bet would sleep on the floor that night. And there was one guy who I won’t name who decided to stay on the bus for about a © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-
year, and he got a little weird as time went on. You could imagine. His friends the dust mites and—
Yeah it gets a little strange.
He probably smelled like a bus for about a year.

Well I mean he’d borrow somebody’s shower for a day every once in a while. But when you’re in your early 20s it’s fun. Now it’s not. And we saw the world, we traveled around, all the big life experiences you get on this thing. Learned how to play cards, and other things that I won’t mention now, but it was a good time and also a real discipline musically. Because I was playing lead alto, and he gave me like a spotlight within the concerts of 15 minutes to just do my own thing on clarinet. He was so nice to me. In fact when I decided to leave the band I was really torn about this. He told me he said, “look you’re not going to learn any more here, you should go to New York.” He made a bunch of phone calls for me. He even tried to set up, they were just forming the Artie Shaw band again, and he set up an interview with the Willard Alexander Agency for me to be the band leader, see they were looking for a clarinet player. But they — you know we never heard of this guy he’s too young. But it was nice of him to even think of this.
